title: Links and Stories
tagline: Singers who knew songs of thousands of lines, and the method that needs no building at all: just a chain of pictures that tells a story.
card: How oral poets kept enormous songs in their heads, and how to chain any list into a story you can retell.
goal: you will learn how to link pictures into a chain, turn the chain into a story, and decide when to use a story and when to use a palace.

left_off.a: A single place in a palace where you put a picture. The plural is loci.

left_off.q: Why does a palace route have to be fixed?
left_off.a: The order of the places gives the order of the list.

left_off.q: Name a good and a bad locus.
left_off.a: Good: a distinctive stove in a well-lit kitchen. Bad: the third of five identical chairs, or a place you have never really looked at.

story.heading: The singers who never learned their songs

text: In the 1930s a young American scholar of Greek, Milman Parry, travelled through the villages and coffee-houses of what was then Yugoslavia, with his assistant Albert Lord and a recording machine. He was looking for something he could not find in a library. He wanted to hear how an epic poem is actually performed by someone who cannot read.

Wherever they went, they found singers, usually men, who sat with a one-stringed instrument called a gusle and sang stories of battles and heroes. Some of these songs were thousands of lines long, and they went on for hours.

check.q: What did Parry want to find out?
check.a: How a long epic poem is performed and kept by singers who cannot read.

parts.talk: Could you sing or tell a story that lasts for hours? What would you need to remember it?

text: Parry and Lord asked the same question again and again: how do you remember so much? The answers surprised them. The singers did not learn the songs word for word. They did not even think they sang the same song twice. Each time, they built the song again as they sang, using a store of stock phrases, familiar scenes (the hero arming himself, the messenger riding out, the feast) and, above all, a strong sense of the story's shape.
The story was the memory. If you know what happens next, you can find the words. If a singer lost his place, he did not stop: he knew the next event and moved on to it.

check.q: How did the singers keep such long songs in mind?
check.a: They did not memorise the words. They remembered the story and its familiar scenes, and rebuilt the song as they sang.

parts.talk: Why do you think a story is easier to remember than a list? Give an example from your own life.

text: Parry and Lord's work changed how scholars think about the poems of Homer, which may have been made in a similar way. For us the lesson is practical. You can use the same power for any list. When you have no palace, or no time, or only a few things to remember, make the items into a story in which each one leads to the next.

This is the link method. It is not as strong as a palace, because if one link breaks the chain can break, but it is quick, it needs no building, and it works anywhere. It is the second great tool in your kit, and in the next rooms you will start to combine it with the others.

check.q: Why is the link method useful?
check.a: It is quick, needs no place, and works for any list, because each item leads to the next in a story.

parts.talk: Tell a short story that connects what you did this morning, step by step. Is it easier than just listing the steps?

words.m: a connection between two things, one after the other in a chain. Each link leads to the next.
a series of connected things. A chain of pictures.
a very long poem or story about heroes and great events.
ready-made and often used. A stock phrase.
to join things together into one fabric or story.
a set of things that come one after another in a particular order.

source: Milman Parry and Albert Lord's field recordings of South Slavic singers were made in the 1930s; Lord's The Singer of Tales (1960) sets out the findings. Retold here in our own words.

method.x: A link is a picture in which two items act on each other. A chain is a row of links. A story is a chain that makes sense of itself.

data.label: A chain of five linked items

method.cap: Item 1 acts on item 2, item 2 on item 3, and so on.

items.h: Make a picture for each item.
items.x: Use what you learned in room 2. Substitute if it is not a thing.
Let them act on each other: the first one hits, rides, eats, drowns or melts the second.
Now item 2 is the active one. Keep the action visible.
Each link only has to hold two pictures. Never try to link item 1 to item 5.
Start with the first picture. It will bring the second, and so on.

method.title: A linked story of five items
lines: A giant red apple rolls downhill, as big as a bicycle wheel, and you chase it on your bicycle.
An elephant jumps in front of you, grabs your bicycle and pedals away.
The elephant picks up an enormous telephone and trumpets into it.
The telephone melts and drips into a volcano, which erupts.
method.pic: An apple rolls; you chase it on a bicycle; an elephant steals the bicycle; it trumpets into a telephone; the telephone melts into a volcano.

try.title: Two links
try.prompt: Link orange → bicycle → cloud. Write what happens between the orange and the bicycle, and between the bicycle and the cloud.
try.model: An orange the size of a beach ball is rolling along the road. It jumps up and lands in the basket of your bicycle, making the front wheel lift. You pedal so hard that the bicycle takes off and rides into a huge pink cloud, leaving a trail of sparkling juice.
checks: Each item acts on the next one.
I did not skip a link.

try.title: A story of four
try.prompt: Make one linked story with these four items, in order: hammer → penguin → pyramid → star.
try.model: You swing a golden hammer and a penguin pops out of the floor, waddling and flapping. The penguin dashes to a pyramid and hits it with its beak. The whole pyramid bursts into dust and a star rises out of the dust, singing.
checks: The four items appear in order.
Each picture is vivid and moving.
I can retell it without looking.

items.s: A picture in which two items act on each other is called a ___.
A row of linked items is a ___.
Never link item 1 to item ___. Link each item only to the next one.

try.q: Which is the better situation for the link method?
opts: A 200-item list you need to jump around in
Six things you need to remember on the way to the shop
A list you want to keep for a year
try.why: A short, quick list is exactly where a story chain is best. For long lists use a palace.

try.title: Palace or story?
pairs: The ten steps of a recipe you will make once tonight

try.title: Tell it
try.prompt: Tell your hammer-penguin-pyramid-star story aloud without looking at the page. Then tell it again, faster.

cards: Items are joined in pairs by pictures in which they act on each other.
A chain of links that makes a story; the plot helps to hold the order.
A forgotten link can break the chain from that point on.
Short lists and sequences; quick jobs; no building needed.
A short chain at each place of a palace: the palace holds the order, the chain holds the detail.
Scholars who found that singers kept thousands of lines by remembering the story, not the words.

quiz.q: What should each link in a chain involve?
opts: Two items acting on each other
quiz.why: A link is made of two things interacting; the chain is made of overlapping pairs.

quiz.q: What is the main weakness of a chain?
opts: One forgotten link can lose the rest
quiz.why: Each item leads to the next, so a missing link may stop you.

quiz.q: What did the epic singers mostly remember?
opts: The shape of the story and its familiar scenes
quiz.why: They rebuilt the song as they sang from the story and stock scenes.

quiz.q: When is the story method best?
opts: For a short list you need quickly, with no place to use
quiz.why: It is quick and flexible for lists of up to about a dozen.

challenge.title: Memory challenge: twelve gods in a story
challenge.intro: Link twelve Greek gods into a single story, in this order: Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Demeter, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Ares, Aphrodite, Hephaestus, Hermes, Dionysus. (Some lists put Hestia instead of Dionysus.) Make the silliest story you can.
challenge.study: Zeus (zoo) hits Hera (a hairy) ... Make each god act on the next one.

look_back.q: Why is a real place better than an invented one for a palace?
look_back.a: You already know it, so you do not have to learn the building as well as the list.

look_back.q: How many body pegs are there, and which is peg 5?
Why do ordinary pictures not stay in memory?
look_back.a: Because nothing about them is surprising. Strange, funny, loud or huge pictures are what we keep.
The pattern that forgetting is fastest at the start and then slows, so early reviews matter most.
